The British Cræft Prize · 2026

A prosthetic limb designed to be shown, not hidden.

Block‑printed, modular, and printed on a machine that fits on a bench. Drag it. Scroll and it comes apart. Press Configure to change whose leg it is.

The premise

Built to vanish,
or to look clinical.

A prosthetic foot is one of the most intimate objects a person can own. Most are designed either to disappear or to look like equipment.

They are mechanically sophisticated. Personal expression is usually an afterthought. I started from a different premise: a prosthesis can be comfortable and technically credible and still be something its wearer chooses to show.

The name comes from the paduka, one of the oldest forms of footwear in India. It is a sole and a toe‑knob, carved from wood, and it never tries to look like a bare foot. That gave me the idea. A prosthesis does not have to imitate the body to belong to the person wearing it.

What it is

Three linked components.

A printable outer form, a system that generates the ornament, and an internal structure that gives the limb flex.

The form is the cuff, shank, ankle and foot, standing on the paduka it clips onto. The wearer picks a tradition, a palette and how much ornament they want, and the software writes the manufacturing geometry. Not a flat image wrapped around a standard foot.

Whose leg is it?

Tone, dye, tradition, and how far the ornament goes. Change any of them and the object changes. Nothing reloads.

This is the whole argument in miniature. Ornament here is a parameter of the geometry rather than a decal on a render, so the numbers redrawing this model are the numbers that redraw the print file. Press Export in the panel and the page writes that file, in the configuration you are looking at, and hands it to Bambu Studio.

Advanced prosthetic feet cost thousands of pounds, and bespoke cosmetic work adds specialist labour on top of that. Once the mechanical core is validated, two wearers can have nothing visual in common and still come off the same production line.

The craft

Three blocks, one register.

A Sanganeri cloth is never one drawing. It is separate carved blocks, one per colour, laid down in order.

Which is what a four‑filament print is: the same manufacturing method, four hundred years apart. The clear ground left between two dyes is the block printer's register gap, and it is also three extrusion widths of unmixed filament. I inherited the rule and then had to measure it.

I chose paisley and Indian block printing because their histories already connect India and Britain. The motif grew from the Kashmiri buta, became desirable here through imported shawls, and was later reproduced at scale by British manufacturers, particularly in Paisley. That history contains both exchange and displacement, and I would rather state the chain than borrow quietly from it.

Material and machine

What the material will hold.

A woodcarver knows what the grain will take. Here, extrusion width, layer height and toolpath do the same job.

Textile patterns cannot simply be shrunk onto a three‑dimensional object. Fine lines disappear below the nozzle width, closely spaced forms merge, isolated details add travel and stringing, and unsupported relief makes waste. So I treat minimum feature width, spacing, island size and overhang as design rules from the start. The printer is not just reproducing a finished design. Its behaviour helps shape one.

1.7 mm minimum line 1.25 mm register gap 1.5 mm inlay depth inlaid, not embossed

The prototypes print in Extrudr WOOD, a wood‑fibre biopolymer made from lignin with spruce and lime. I chose it for the history. James Potts's Anglesey Leg of about 1830, widely taken as Britain's first modern prosthetic, is catalogued by the National Trust as lime wood and vegetable‑tanned leather, and lime was also the timber of British ornamental carving. The same wood sits in the history of artificial limbs and in the history of fine ornament. What I actually want is a lime‑derived fibre in a printable composite, and nobody sells one.

The joint

The change that came from listening.

I spoke to disabled people through care groups and to people with experience of NHS services. Comfort came up every time.

That exposed the weakness of a rigid printed foot. It could be visually distinctive and inexpensive and still fail as a prosthesis. So the foot now comes apart at the ankle, and the pin sits at the height of the malleoli, because the malleoli are the ends of the bones the pin replaces. The ankle on screen is moving now, through its real travel, about its real axis. Two bumpers do the tuning: the rear one compresses as the heel lands so the foot comes flat instead of slapping, and the front one pushes back as you roll off it.

The benchmark is the energy return of a modern carbon‑fibre foot. I am not claiming this matches one. The question is how much of that behaviour additive manufacturing can reproduce at a much lower manufacturing cost. That is roughly the question the Jaipur Foot asked in 1968, when P. K. Sethi and Ram Chandra Sharma built a foot around squatting, sitting cross‑legged and walking barefoot over uneven ground. It showed me that prosthetic design is never culturally neutral.

Voices

Three people who moved the design.

As an amputee who enjoys artwork like realism and mannerism, I believe this solves a big problem, mainly cost‑wise. I enjoy this design style and think many people would like to express themselves with this generation technology.
Arun JamesAmputee · Cold War veteran, 77
I really like the Indian design and learning about the paduka tradition. I would definitely use this prosthetic leg. But an important consideration is you should design the leg to make walking easier.
Jane ChurchAmputee, 71
I believe there is a market for this product, though authorising this to become a medical device will take roughly half a year, and you need to ensure these materials are biodegradable. I like the designs though.
Shenqu QiaoOrthotist · NHS Addenbrooke's

Jane's note is why the ankle exists. Shenqu's is why the regulatory path and the biopolymer are stated plainly here rather than glossed over. Each conversation removed an assumption I had made. The form came from footwear history, the prosthetic function came from studying culturally specific design, and the flex came from listening to the people who would wear it.

Honest status

What works, and what does not.

Ornament engine — works, measured Printed prototype — six pieces, assembles Single‑axis ankle — travel verified Stiffness & energy return — not yet measured Lime‑fibre composite — does not exist yet Clinical validation — needs partners

The ornament method and the printable geometry can be demonstrated now. To take it further the flexible architecture has to be prototyped and measured against established prosthetic feet, and the structural material, fatigue performance and clinical validation all still need development. This is not a certified load‑bearing prosthesis and I am not presenting it as one.

The longer‑term model is simple. The wearer chooses their preferences, the system writes the file, the file travels, and the object is made close to them. That should cut transport and inventory while putting personalisation within reach. Computation goes where repetition is expensive, and fitting, comfort and clinical judgement stay human work.

What I want is a prosthetic foot that is cheaper to personalise, can be made locally, and is beautiful enough that people are proud to show it off. Heritage craft as a working design system, not a visual reference.
